av_event.line_text: Everything's targets. I just tell them straight if a number's daft. Doesn't make me popular.
av_event.what: A man in a work T-shirt walks across the kitchen behind Gemma, opens the fridge-freezer, takes something out and leaves the frame; Gemma does not turn round.

text:
A: Alright? I'm Darren. Can you hear me okay? This laptop's older than my daughter, near enough.
B: Yeah, I can hear you. I'm Gemma.
A: Lovely. Where's that to then, Gemma, where are you?
B: Sutton-in-Ashfield. Nottinghamshire. Between Mansfield and Nottingham, sort of.
A: Oh right, I've been through Mansfield, I think, years back. I'm Bridgwater, Somerset. Bottom left, basically. Did you do that puzzle thing at the start?
B: Yeah. Didn't finish it.
A: No, me neither, mate. I got about three in and thought, er, I'll just guess the rest. I'm better with my hands than all that, you know. What do you do for work?
B: I manage a builders' merchants. Timber, plumbing, heating. Trade counter and a yard.
A: No way! That's funny, that, 'cause I started in a builders' merchant. Yard lad at sixteen, straight out of school, stayed there years till they laid us off. Now I'm on flooring and tiles at one of the big DIY places in Taunton. So we're sort of the same line, aren't we, except your lot know what they're buying and mine don't.
B: Pretty much. Trade are easier in some ways. They know what they want. They just argue about the price.
A: Ha, yeah. I had a fella last week, wanted to tile a whole bathroom in an afternoon. Floor and walls. Never held a trowel in his life. I said to him, mate, I've been doing this twenty-odd years and I wouldn't do it in an afternoon. Sold him the stuff anyway, mind, but I talked him out of the dear adhesive. He didn't need it.
B: See, that's where you'd get in bother with my regional manager.
A: Upselling, is it?
B: Everything's targets. I just tell them straight if a number's daft. Doesn't make me popular.
A: No, I bet. They asked me to go team leader, I said no thanks. I'd rather be on the floor than doing rotas. Do you like it, managing?
B: Erm. I like the job. Not sure I like the managing bit. I got it 'cause I knew the stock better than anyone, not 'cause I wanted to be in charge of people. And the paperwork, I'm terrible. My assistant, Dawn, she basically keeps me alive.
A: Oh, don't talk to me about paperwork. My supervisor's had words about me not logging stuff on the handheld. I just forget, I'm too busy chatting. Everyone needs a Dawn, don't they.
B: Everyone needs a Dawn.
A: Here, I saw your jigsaw on the table in your photo. How long's that been there?
B: Since Easter.
A: Easter! That's dedication, that is.
B: Thousand pieces. It's mostly sky. I do a bit when I've had a rubbish day. Lee keeps putting his tea on it.
A: Is Lee your other half?
B: Husband. He's an electrician. Leaves his tools all down the hallway.
A: Ha, my shed's the same, never tidy it. Donna, my wife, she's given up on me. What do you do outside of work then? Bit of telly?
B: Crime books, mainly. Walk the dog round the reservoir. She's old, Mabel, got arthritis, so it's slow.
A: Oh, ours is the same! Pickle, Jack Russell, he's fourteen and grumpy as anything. Takes him ten minutes to decide which way to go along the river. What's yours?
B: Staffie. Costs me a fortune in tablets.
A: They do, don't they. Worth it, mind. Do you go away much, holidays?
B: Caravan. Mablethorpe usually. Same place every year. I'm not fussed about abroad, airports do my head in.
A: You and me both! We do a caravan in Cornwall most summers. Did Tenerife twice for anniversaries, and honestly, the queues at Bristol, I'd rather—
